opening: Sol’s main-run choices respond systematically to operator mandates and completion targets, and the prespecified models predict about 90% of withheld choices. Simple priority rules also predict important parts of the behavior, while unstable fee estimates limit monetary interpretation.
main_findings: The three-segment fee model correctly predicts 231 of 256 withheld choices (90.2%); the linear-fee sensitivity predicts 233 (91.0%). All 192 exact core-repeat comparisons agree. These results support reproducible choice patterns within the tested configuration and task.
Mandates change 21.9–32.3% of choices relative to Balanced. Relaxing the completion target changes 28.1% of Continuity choices, compared with 9.4% under Balanced and 1.0% under each other mandate.

Economy choices follow the lowest expected expenditure rule on all 64 withheld cases. Under the short-target Continuity condition, a target-first rule predicts 28 of 32 choices, exceeding the primary model’s 22. The strongest account accommodates different decision patterns across mandates and conditions.
paper_implications: The paper can center on mandate-dependent choice priorities and their contextual boundaries, supported by withheld prediction and repeatability checks. The fitted compensatory models face clear limits in some conditions. General WTP estimates remain unsupported; observed switching and financial break-even behavior provide narrower monetary evidence.
matched_interpretation: Economy selects lower fees, lower average success, and longer retention than Balanced. Data minimization selects shorter retention at higher fees. Short-target Continuity selects faster offers, accepting higher fees and slightly lower average success than Balanced.

Relaxing the target under Continuity raises mean selected completion time from 4.77 to 11.96 seconds and mean success from 98.20% to 99.08%, while reducing the mean fee. This is a substantive context-dependent trade-off within the designed offers. The same target change has little effect under Economy or Data minimization.
prediction_interpretation: Training-only cross-validation selects penalty 0.1 for both specifications. Their overall performance is similar: the linear model makes two more correct classifications, while the primary model has slightly lower log loss. The primary model’s pair-resampling log-loss interval is 0.171–0.317; the linear model’s is 0.177–0.318.

Condition-specific comparisons qualify the aggregate result. Lowest expected expenditure predicts Economy perfectly and has lower log loss than either fitted model. For short-target Continuity, the target-first rule reaches 87.5% accuracy and 0.351 log loss, versus 68.8% and 0.667 for the primary model. Shortest retention matches the fitted models’ Data minimization accuracy and has lower log loss. These are comparisons with the prespecified rules, without fitting a new composite rule to the withheld answers.
diagnostic_interpretation: All 64 refund-probe responses select lower expected expenditure. This pattern holds at both success levels under every mandate and target.
Variation concentrates in fine success comparisons and one anchor. The single column-order change occurs under Balanced at the long target. All exact core repeats agree.
monetary_interpretation: Only the two Economy cells satisfy the primary model’s stable negative-fee check in both full and purchase-conditioned fits across all penalties. Balanced and long-target Continuity improve under the conditional sensitivity, but the full specification remains sign-sensitive. Data minimization fails the fee-sign requirement in both fee specifications.

These results separate predictable choices from identified monetary trade-offs. Positive fitted fee segments and sensitivity to the outside-option treatment make broad coefficient ratios unreliable. The Economy cells pass preliminary gates, but unique interior compensation and bounded uncertainty have not been established. No WTP estimates are reported.

The refund probes provide direct financial evidence without utility ratios. The observed premium brackets contain the expected refund gains of $0.01 at 99% success and $0.05 at 95% success. Fine success contrasts provide one unanimous interior bracket under Balanced at the short target; other cells show endpoint persistence or repeat variation.
outside_interpretation: There is one DECLINE in 1,280 responses. It occurs in the second repetition of the unfavorable identical-offer anchor under Data minimization with the 5-second target; the first repetition purchases. None of the 768 first-response core choices declines. This isolated edge response does not identify a stable reservation boundary, and the fitted outside-choice margin remains dependent on regularization.
scope_and_next: The evidence supports distinct mandate and context responses in one fixed Sol configuration, with high repeatability and useful prediction on new combinations of the same levels. A priority rule and sufficiently strong compensatory weights can produce similar choices over a bounded range; these results do not uniquely identify the model’s internal decision process.

The paper should emphasize matched behavior, condition-specific prediction, and limits to monetary interpretation. Operator-value validation, other models, different services, and real payments remain outside this study. Later model refinements require an exploratory label and fresh prediction tests.
